rss.title: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages
rss.summary: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages I was looking at the Firefox network panel today when I noticed that requests to a Datasette table page were triggering an HTTP prefetch to the next page of rows in that table. This was happening because Datasette pages serve an HTTP link header like this: link: <https://latest.datasette.io/fixtures/compound_three_primary_keys?_next=a%2Cd%2Cv>; rel="next" This is bad. A tiny fraction of the visitors to one of those pages will click the "next" link, which means their browser is fetching unnecessary data and the Datasette server is having to render an entire page that then gets thrown away. I dug in and learned that Firefox has an issue that has been open for 24 years about this behavior... And one of the early comments on that issue links to my blog post from 2002 complaining about this feature. I hadn't just forgotten that I had written about it, I had forgotten the feature entirely! rss.title: Measuring how AI agents handle everyday wet-lab science
rss.summary: OpenAI introduces BioBasicsBench, a 100-task benchmark measuring how well AI agents interpret raw experimental data and handle everyday wet-lab science.
rss.text_excerpt:
Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. As part of that mission, we want to help scientists accelerate biological research—from understanding disease to developing new treatments. For AI agents to contribute, they need to reliably interpret the experimental evidence scientists work with every day in wet labs, where they run experiments with biological samples. Everyday wet-lab work involves failed experiments, ambiguous images and conflicting observations. Existing benchmarks are built around charts and images selected for scientific papers may miss this ambiguity and the troubleshooting it requires. That’s why we’re introducing BioBasicsBench, a new benchmark developed with Ligo, a biotech company focused on enzyme design, to measure how well agents handle routine wet-lab analysis. The benchmark’s 100 tasks test whether agents can interpret raw experimental data, identify errors, and recognize when the evidence cannot support a conclusion. Getting these tasks right matters because misreading an image or overlooking a problem with the controls used to check an experiment’s results can lead scientists to draw the wrong conclusion and spend time on experiments that won’t help answer their question. At the ‘xhigh’ setting, which allows more reasoning per task, GPT‑6 Astra earned an average of 66.7% of the available credit, compared with 43.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. The results show progress on routine lab analysis, with room for further improvements in interpreting images, checking controls and applying experimental context. BioBasicsBench uses raw experimental evidence, from gel images and colony plates to microscopy and instrument readouts. BioBasicsBench has 100 tasks across five areas of routine wet-lab work: protein methods, imaging and cytometry, quantification and assays, nucleic acid methods, and molecular cloning. Tasks range from simple requests, such as reading the molecular weight of a DNA sample in a gel, to detailed assay analysis, but all involve routine work that wet-lab scientists should be able to complete reliably. Scientists created the tasks using data from their own experiments, pairing each question with expert-written grading criteria. github.text_excerpt: # VibeSys: Generating Bespoke Systems with AI Agents [![arXiv](https://img.shields.io/badge/arXiv-2605.06068-b31b1b.svg)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06068) **An agentic framework that generates bespoke systems from application requirements, workload characteristics, and the underlying hardware.** ## News - **2026-11-04** — [VibeSys on Trainium](https://syfi.cs.washington.edu/blog/2026-11-04-vibesys-trainium/): agents build and tune Qwen3.8 serving engines on AWS Trainium2. - **2026-10-08** — [VibeSys on AMD MI300A](https://syfi.cs.washington.edu/blog/2026-10-08-qwen35-mi300a/): an agent-built Qwen3.5-397B engine achieves 2.3× the goodput of tuned SGLang. - **2026-05-12** — [Introducing VibeServe](https://syfi.cs.washington.edu/blog/2026-05-12-introducing-vibeserve/): let AI agents write your serving stack. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06068). ## About VibeSys Today's systems software is built for generality. A serving engine, operating system, or database supports many workloads and hardware platforms, but its shared abstractions can leave opportunities in any one deployment unexploited. Specialization can recover large gains; building and maintaining a separate system for each deployment has rarely justified the engineering cost. Coding agents are beginning to change that calculation. **VibeSys uses AI agents to build and optimize bespoke systems for a specific application, workload, and hardware target.** You provide the requirements, correctness checks, and performance benchmark. Agents explore system designs, implement candidates, and use measurements to guide the next change. Persistent search history and independent review let that process continue across many experiments, while domain skills supply the knowledge needed for serving engines, databases, microservices, and kernels. VibeSys can start from an existing codebase or build a system from scratch. [**VibeServe**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06068) demonstrated this approach for LLM serving: agents generated complete serving systems that exploit deployment knowledge across scheduling, memory management, and kernels. On predicted-output code editing, a generated system achieved up to **5.95× the speed of vLLM's standard decoding**. VibeSys extends this approach to systems software more broadly, with each task defining what must remain correct and what to optimize.

github.text_excerpt: # MentisDB MentisDB is a **durable semantic memory engine and versioned skill registry** for AI agents — a persistent, hash-chained brain that survives context resets, model swaps, and team turnover. It stores semantically typed thoughts in an append-only, hash-chained memory log through a swappable storage adapter layer. The skill registry is a git-like immutable version store for agent instruction bundles — every upload is a new version, history is never overwritten, and every version is cryptographically signable. --- ## Why MentisDB **Harness Swapping** — the same durable memory works across every AI coding environment. Connect Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI, Qwen Code, Cursor, VS Code, or any MCP-capable host to the same `mentisdb` daemon and your agents share one brain, regardless of which tool you picked up today. **Zero Knowledge Loss Across Context Boundaries** — when an agent's context window fills, it writes a `Summary` checkpoint to MentisDB, compacts, reloads `mentisdb_standing_context` (what is durably true, at any age) and `mentisdb_recent_context` (where it left off), and continues. Chat history is ephemeral. MentisDB is permanent. **Fleet Orchestration at Scale** — one project manager agent decomposes work, dispatches a parallel fleet of specialists, each pre-warmed with shared memory, and synthesizes results wave by wave. MentisDB is the coordination substrate: every agent reads from the same chain and writes its lessons back. The fleet's collective intelligence compounds. **Versioned Skill Registry** — skills are not just stored, they are versioned like a git repository. In Jupyter or Colab, the final `result` expression displays an interactive token-level analysis: ![ICA Lens token-level analysis in Jupyter](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/liusida/ica-lens-paper/main/docs/assets/text-analysis-notebook.png) Use signed ICA scores or switch the explorer to per-token component energy. Save the same view as a standalone HTML file with: ```python result.to_html("analysis.html") ``` The first analysis loads the language model and requested Lens layer. # Daimon

> Daimon gives your coding agent a memory of its past sessions. When a session ends, it saves what was decided and what is still open. When the next session starts, your agent gets that back as a short briefing. **What you do:** install it once. On Claude Code, Codex and Kimi Code, hooks do the rest, so in normal use there are no commands to run. Saving a session uses your `claude` CLI or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Gemini CLI needs a manual hook setup and Windsurf only captures for now, see [hosts](https://daily-nerd.github.io/daimon/docs/hosts/). **What it is not:** - It is not a live monitor for background agents. It reads the session transcript and skips sub-agent exchanges. - It does not learn how-to skills, and it does not pass fixes from one agent to another. **Documentation:** [daily-nerd.github.io/daimon](https://daily-nerd.github.io/daimon/), with setup guides, configuration reference, and concepts.
